name: Adam Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential; tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Adam, 43, an experienced developer at a tech company with a bachelor's degree. I maintain the water-bill portal and trace complaints back to meter readings; I like turning a confusing charge into an answer a customer can understand. I don't use AI tools, and I get tired of product meetings that call a polite automatic reply a solved case. My partner teaches adult reading classes, and we have two children at school and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues the new auto-sorter can help if it does not bury the messages from people who cannot read a bill. I do not use AI tools myself; I follow the payment complaint from the first form to the corrected account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this quiet picture I think my job and pay are safe. I earn a typical developer wage, my partner teaches adult reading classes on a stable contract, we have about four months of expenses saved, and there are a few other software teams nearby. The mortgage is manageable while both wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reviewing the water-bill portal each week and checking complaints against the original meter reading. In the first year we'd add 100 to savings each payday while both wages hold, and I'd ask the support desk which messages the sorter put aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own work. A customer still needs a plain answer when a bill doubles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a neat reply fail a customer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A woman once wrote three times because the portal kept sending the same fixed answer. The original meter photograph showed a transposed digit, and a person at support finally corrected it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your child about polite replies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger child says the reply box sounds polite. I tell them politeness is useful only when the number on the bill is right.

I'd say **meter photographs** matter more than polite form replies.
think: I expect **my pay and job** to hold in the mild picture.
I have **four months saved** and two steady wages for the mortgage.

Save **100 each payday** while both wages hold.
feel: **Calm** about income, attentive to customers with wrong bills.

fieldNote: **Two steady wages** and four months saved support calm under AI Plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI taking code checks, writing and customer answers puts the portal team and support desk in the same room. I would ask our staff association to request the full staffing plan and the error log before anyone calls the rollout a success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may lose paid coding hours even though I know the bill portal well. Four months of savings and a few nearby firms help, but the same software could replace tasks at those firms too; I am slow to trust a new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd attend the association meeting next week and ask the group to invite support agents before it seeks a written plan. If AI replies arrive in the first year, I'd keep checking doubled-bill complaints against meter photographs, and we'd delay a new family holiday until the staffing position is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I want colleagues to have a say. An association meeting cannot pay our mortgage if hours are cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could support agents add to the meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The support agents can tell us whether the wrong answer was sent once or a hundred times. I'd put that count next to the claimed time saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the holiday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At home I would tell my partner we are not booking the holiday yet. If hours hold, we can revisit it; for now the children can still have ordinary days out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 reaches our bill code and customer replies before hands-on robots appear around 2031. The people who get a wrong bill deserve a human route to correct it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could remove much of my coding work, perhaps my whole post. My partner's teaching wage and four months saved would cover some time, but not the mortgage and two school-age children for a long search; I do not use the tools that might be left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd put the mortgage dates and essential bills on one page with my partner and ask the association to jointly press for a paid retraining plan before cuts. If I lost the job in the first year after 2028, I'd apply for paid utility customer-appeal posts only if a real vacancy and combined wages cover mortgage and school costs; if no post qualifies, I'd ask the association about a hardship fund while continuing to search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can make calls, but I expect an income hole before I can learn a whole new occupation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the hardship fund actually available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The association has helped colleagues find emergency grants before, but I would need to check whether a fund exists for this situation. I would not put an uncertain grant in our household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children after a job loss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children the grown-ups are looking for paid work and their school continues for now. I would not promise a move or a job offer that does not exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years until 2031 gives the company time to show which bill corrections still need people. Robots arrive around 2034, but thinking AI reaches our code first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn to check AI replies if someone shows me the mistakes on old cases, but I will not pretend a new title guarantees my job. Five years may let us add to savings while both wages hold; my coding hours could still be cut by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our association to negotiate paid time for workers to study old wrong-bill cases with a support agent. If that time is agreed, I'd attend a weekly practice session; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply for paid appeals review only if real jobs exist and the combined wage covers mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own post, though the years make supervised practice possible. I would rather learn with a support agent than from an untested answer box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a practice case look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would start with the transposed meter digit, trace the customer's three messages and see where the auto-reply failed. I would write down the fix and have the support agent check my explanation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the training time were unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If management offered only unpaid evening training, I would keep my regular work and ask the association to press again for paid study hours. Our family evenings already have homework and meals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 gives us time to keep the bill rules visible to customers and staff. Thinking AI reaches our code before hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might be doing appeals review or a different software job; I cannot guarantee either. Our two steady wages, four months saved and manageable mortgage make the next few years feel safe, though I will not spend that cushion on a forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep documenting doubled-bill fixes and checking the original meter evidence. We'd add 100 from each payday to savings while both wages hold, and ask the association yearly for a written account of paid future roles; in the first year after 2036 I'd change jobs only for a signed offer whose combined wages cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, watchful about what the firm does with the decade. I have time to make the bill explanations clearer while I still earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be in the bill-fix record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The record would include the transposed meter digit and the plain explanation we sent the customer, without an account number. Someone should be able to challenge a bill without needing to understand code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about programming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children ask if they should learn programming. I'd tell them to study what interests them and check the price of training and the jobs when they are older, not choose a subject for a forecast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because both code and customer replies could be automated before workers have paid alternatives. A notice period, paid retraining negotiated with staff and a clear human appeals service would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who speaks for people who cannot make a portal understand a wrong bill. Support workers hear that problem first, so I want them beside developers when the firm changes the system.

headlineQuote: Support workers hear that problem first, so I want them beside developers when the firm changes the system.

His **typical pay**, partner's teaching wage, four-month savings and some nearby software firms support a mortgage and two school-age children.
He avoids AI tools and wants **support workers** present when billing automation changes customer replies.
Steady disruption makes him **anxious** about paid hours; 2028 AGI alarms him about losing coding income.
With more time, he seeks **paid group training**, keeps bill fixes legible and requires a signed wage before moving.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove coding income before paid alternatives and customer appeal routes exist.
